entities.name: Angelo Rotta
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Angelo Rotta (1872–1965) served as the Apostolic Nuncio to Hungary from 1930 to 1945, becoming a pivotal figure in the Catholic Church's humanitarian efforts during the Holocaust. His strategic diplomatic position in Budapest placed him at the epicenter of a desperate struggle to protect the city's Jewish population from Nazi Germany's systematic extermination campaign, directly challenging the genocidal policies of Adolf Eichmann and the Arrow Cross Party. Rotta's actions transcended traditional diplomatic roles, establishing him as a courageous resistor against totalitarian evil, embodying a moral defiance that saved thousands of lives.

During the climactic final year of World War II, as the Soviet Red Army advanced and the Nazi regime tightened its grip on Hungary, Archbishop Rotta orchestrated a complex network of rescue operations. He issued protective passports (Schutzpässe) under Vatican auspices, designating their holders as wards of the Holy See, and established safe houses throughout Budapest, including the Vatican Nunciature itself. Collaborating with other neutral diplomats like Carl Lutz of Switzerland, Raoul Wallenberg of Sweden, and Giorgio Perlasca, Rotta's office coordinated the distribution of thousands of these documents, providing sanctuary and a semblance of legal protection against deportation to Auschwitz.

The legacy of Angelo Rotta extends beyond the immediate cessation of hostilities, profoundly influencing post-war perceptions of the Catholic Church's role during the Holocaust. His unwavering commitment to humanitarian principles, often in direct contravention of German and Hungarian fascist authorities, earned him posthumous recognition as Righteous Among the Nations by Yad Vashem in 1997. Rotta's example stands as a testament to the power of individual moral courage within institutional frameworks, inspiring continued dialogue on diplomatic responsibility and resistance to genocide.
